note: Start with a C5/C6 split, then separate the light and heavy groups into blend/pure product windows to establish the main plant economics.
Start with a complete sequence producing the C3–C6 blends and pure heavy products, using a higher-resolution column only for the difficult C6 paraffin/naphthene split.
Build an initial eight-column sequence: sell C3–C6 blends where attractive, recover ethane and the three heavy paraffins, and use moderate staging/reflux to assess purity and costs.
Start with a C4/C5 split to recover valuable C5+ products while keeping light ends available for blend products.
Start with a C5/C6 split to isolate the two highest-value regions and establish column cost and separation sharpness.
Start with a sharp C4/C5 split to recover the valuable C5+ material while assessing column costs and achievable purity.
Build the blend-oriented base case and measure purity, recovery, and costs across all nine separations.
Start with a full volatility sequence producing light blends, a C5 blend, C6 naphthenes, and heavy products; use moderate separations to establish purity and cost tradeoffs.

Start with a four-column sequence discarding the low-value light cut and producing saleable C5, C6-paraffin, and C6-naphthene blends. Moderate staging and reflux establish purity and cost before tuning.

Reconfigure around high-value C3–C6 blend cuts: remove ethane, isolate C4 and C5 blends, then split C6 paraffins from naphthenes. This should generate five substantial revenue streams with only six columns.
The feed column failed to converge at high pressure. Lower its pressure and add stages and reflux/boil-up to obtain a robust initial split.
Reset to a single sharp C5/C6 split, shifting the distillate cut heavier so the valuable C6-and-heavier material is isolated first.

Build the full direct sequence: recover C4 and C5 blends, C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, then heptane, octane and nonane. Discard the low-value ethane/C3 overhead rather than pay for a refrigerated deethanizer.
Start with a split between the C5 and C6 families; this keeps the light and heavy processing problems separate and gives a basis for tuning the plant.
Sharpen the C4/C5 split, then test C3/C4 and C5/C6 splits so the major blend products can be sold.
Reduce boil-up to make the feed column a sharp C4/C5 split; the previous cut carried too much pentane overhead.
Recover convergence with a simpler, lower-pressure feed split before rebuilding the downstream train.

Restructure to four high-value blend cuts: C4/C5 at the feed, C3/C4, C5/C6, then C6 paraffins from heavier material. This removes low-value heavy-product columns and should greatly improve revenue per column.
Sharpen the existing sequence into C4/C5, C5/C6, C6/C7, and C7/C8 cuts so the C5 and C6 cuts can qualify as blends.
Reconfigure the plant around the valuable C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blends: sharpen the feed and C5 cuts, add deethanization and C3/C4 splitting, and simplify the heavy-product sequence.
Build a blend-oriented flowsheet around the C5/C6 split, with tuned distillate-to-bottoms ratios and a final heptane recovery column.
Simplify to one column and sharpen the C4/C5 split; the current low-reflux cascade produces no saleable stream and is far too expensive.
Build a four-column train to recover C5 blend, C4 blend, and a C3-rich stream while lowering pressures to reduce expensive energy and refrigeration.
Concentrate on the valuable C5 and C6 products: make a clean C4/C5 cut, then a much sharper C5/C6 cut, while dropping the low-value light-end column.
Split both primary products into saleable carbon-number blends: C3/C4 overhead and C5/C6+ in the bottoms, using moderate reflux to control cost.
Build a five-column blend train: C3/C4, C5, C6 paraffins, and C6 naphthenes, leaving C7+ unsold initially. The root is rebalanced to keep C5 in the bottoms.

Build a sharper blend-oriented flowsheet: C3 and C4 light products, then high-value C5, C6 paraffin, and C6 naphthene cuts. Moderate pressure drops should improve volatility while keeping condenser temperatures reasonable.
Rebuild as a full value-oriented sequence: discard only the light C3 cut, sell C4/C5/C6 blends, and recover heptane, octane, and nonane with moderate-size columns.
Simplify to a two-column C5 recovery plant: split C4 and lighter overhead from a saleable C5 blend, avoiding the costly heavy-end columns until the core economics are established.
Prune the unprofitable light and heavy branches and recover the high-value C5 blend from TB, leaving a compact four-column plant.
Concentrate on three high-value blend products. Sharpen the C5/C6, C4/C5, and C6-paraffin/heavy splits while removing unprofitable downstream columns.
Target the valuable C6 paraffin blend with two moderate-duty columns: first remove C5 and lighter material, then split the paraffins from naphthenes and C7+.

Rebalance the cuts to isolate C5 and C6-paraffin blend pools rather than processing every light component. The first column rejects C4 and lighter, the second rejects naphthenes and heavier, and the third splits the two valuable blends.
Sharpen both key cuts enough to sell the C4/C5 region; the present C5/C6 column is losing almost half its tops to C6 contamination, so both reflux and boil-up need a substantial increase.

Build a blend-oriented train: remove ethane from the C3 product and make sharp C4/C5, C5/C6-paraffin, paraffin/naphthene, and naphthene/heavy splits. Higher reflux and reduced feed boil-up are intended to eliminate the cross-contamination that made every current stream unsaleable.
Retune the three downstream splits to their blend boundaries: C5 overhead, C6 paraffins overhead, then C6 naphthenes overhead, while reducing unnecessary boil-up.
Simplify to three columns targeting the two most valuable blends: C5 and C6 paraffins. Discard the low-value light overhead and heavy bottoms to avoid their costly separation trains.

Rebuild into six sharp cuts: discard the light C3/C4 top, then sell C5, C6-paraffin, and C6-naphthene blends plus heptane, octane, and nonane. Higher reflux should eliminate the cross-contamination that made every prior stream unsaleable.
Target a single high-value C5 blend: first reject C4 and lighter overhead, then take C5 overhead from the heavy stream. Removing the light-end column saves substantial cost while I tune the two cuts.
Match each column’s distillate-to-feed ratio to the intended cut, lower pressures to reduce refrigeration cost, and sell the C5 stream directly as a blend once its split is sharpened.
Push each cut to its intended blend boundary and add a C3/C4 column; this should monetise the C3, C4, C5 and C6-paraffin blends.
Increase the first column’s boil-up so all C5 material moves overhead, leaving a clean C6+ bottoms stream; the second column can then recover the high-value C6 paraffin blend.
Build a focused four-column train for the valuable C4, C5, and C6-paraffin blends, with sharp cuts at the C4/C5, C5/C6, and C6-paraffin/naphthene boundaries.
Make the feed column a genuinely sharp C4/C5 split; this should unlock the C4, C5, and C6-blend products downstream without adding equipment.
Sharpen the two product splits enough to cross the 95% blend thresholds; the C5 and C6 paraffin revenues should then outweigh the added column cost.

Repurpose the sequence to make C4, C5, C6-paraffin, and C6-naphthene blends, then recover heptane, octane, and nonane. Lower reflux and eliminate pressure drop should sharply reduce cost and refrigeration.
Sharpen the first cut so essentially all C4 and lighter material goes overhead; this should leave the second column’s overhead as a saleable C5 blend rather than a butane-contaminated stream.
Simplify to three columns targeting the two most valuable products: recover the C5 blend from TB and make a direct C6-paraffin cut in BT, eliminating the costly extra C6 column.
Return to the robust C5/C6 split and recover only the two most valuable blends, C5 and C6 paraffin, using smaller lower-reflux columns to control costs.
Build a three-column sequence to sell the C5 and C6-paraffin blends: split C4/C5 overhead and use a sharper second split between N-hexane and methylcyclopentane.
Switch to a direct-sequence train that sells the C5 and C6-paraffin blends. Use higher pressure and smaller light-end columns to avoid the severe refrigeration and energy costs of the current design.
Make the C4/C5 and C5/C6 cuts sharp enough to sell the valuable C4 and C5 blends, and add a C3/C4 split to recover both light blends.
Simplify to three blend-producing columns: C3/C4 overhead, C5 blend overhead, and unsold C6+ bottoms. Lower pressures and stronger splits should improve purity while eliminating three costly columns.
Cut refrigeration and equipment costs while sharpening the C5 and C6 blend splits; retain the profitable C4 branch and test whether this leaner train can earn a positive return.
Sharpen the light-column split to reject most N-butane overhead and qualify the large C5 bottoms stream as a blend.
Simplify to a robust two-column C6-paraffin recovery: first reject C5 and lighter, then separate the four C6 paraffins from naphthenes and heavier material.
Increase both reboil ratios to recover nearly all C5 overhead while trimming stages and reflux. The target is a 95%+ C5 blend at BT with much lower operating cost.
Sharpen the C5 cut at nearly the same material split and reduce the C6 distillate rate just enough to exclude naphthenes, aiming to make both high-value blends saleable.
Sharpen all three blend-boundary splits substantially. The current column sizes are adequate structurally, but their reflux is far too low to reach the 95% C5 and C6-paraffin blend specifications.
Focus on a robust two-column C5-blend recovery: remove C4 and lighter components, then separate C5 from C6+ with moderate stages and reflux to control cost.
Recover from the non-converged high-reflux design with a much cheaper, robust C5/C6 cut, then use its stream compositions to build only the valuable downstream separations.
Sharpen both carbon-number cuts by increasing boil-up: the goal is C4-free C5 blend overhead from B and C5-free C4 material in the root tops, unlocking the two largest blend revenues.
Sharpen every blend boundary and add an ethane/C3 splitter so all five intended products can qualify. Higher reflux is paired with lower boil-up where heavy leakage was limiting purity.
Return to the best three-column design before the excessive light-column reflux destroyed C5 blend purity.
Simplify to one robust column with a liquid side draw targeting the valuable three-component C6-paraffin blend, avoiding the costly full sequence.

Force much sharper C4/C5 and C5/C6 splits with higher boil-up while reducing column size. The goal is an approximately 695 mol/s C5 blend overhead at BT, with all lighter material rejected at T and C6+ retained at BB.
Concentrate the remaining budget on the two saleable blends: increase C5 and C6-paraffin cut sharpness while reducing the expensive feed column's size and refrigeration demand.

Make the three blend-boundary cuts genuinely sharp, with a heavier distillate cut in the first two columns. This should turn the C5 and C6-paraffin streams into saleable blends and may also qualify the C3/C4 stream for further recovery.
Sharpen the light-ends split and recover the C4, C5, and C6-paraffin blends in a compact three-column sequence.
Reconfigure to a direct sequence: split C5 from C6 at the feed, recover the C5 blend from the light stream, and recover the C6-paraffin blend from the heavy stream.
Build a three-column blend recovery train: split C4 from C5, remove the C3 lights, and isolate the high-value C5 blend from C6 and heavier material.
Reset to a lean four-column blend train with much lower pressure and duty: sharp C4/C5, C3/C4, C5/C6, and C6-paraffin/heavy cuts should yield three high-value blend products.
Raise boil-up at every blend boundary to recover the light product currently leaking into each bottoms stream; keep the existing stage counts and reflux to isolate the recovery effect.
Remove the light-ends column: neither of its outlets sells, so its $244M/yr cost is pure loss while the valuable C6 paraffin product is unchanged.
Make the C4/C5 and C5/C6 separations genuinely sharp, while using pressure letdown to avoid very cold condensers. If both cuts are clean, BT should be the valuable C5 blend.
Push dimethylbutane into TT while retaining the pentanes in TB, and slightly reduce reflux to offset the higher boil-up; this should make the valuable C5 blend saleable.

Reduce the very high equipment and energy costs while shifting the feed-column distillate heavier to capture all n-pentane. The downstream cuts are also rebalanced toward their intended C3/C4+5 and C6-paraffin/heavy boundaries.
Return to a robust two-column C5 recovery scheme with lower stage counts and duties, while removing the failed downstream column.

Sharpen all three cuts and move the boundaries to C5/C6, C4/C5, and C6-paraffin/C6-naphthene. Higher pressure should reduce refrigeration cost while the larger boil-up rates correct the heavy-component leakage overhead.
Use much lower column pressure to improve relative volatility and reduce the severe C5/C6 leakage, while adding stages only on the two high-value cuts.

Strip the plant back to two columns and concentrate on the valuable C5 blend. Lower boil-up and stronger reflux should keep C5 out of the root tops and C6 out of the C5 product while cutting energy cost.
Revert to the best converged five-column blend train before testing targeted purity improvements.
Recover the valuable C5 blend from the unsold light overhead with a C4/C5 split; this should add substantial revenue while preserving the profitable C6 paraffin cut.
Build a lean four-column train to recover the three high-value C5/C6 blends while leaving low-value lights and heavies unsold. Moderate stages and reflux should keep costs below product value.

Switch to the more valuable C6-paraffin blend and keep both columns at feed pressure to avoid refrigeration. The first column rejects C5 and lighter material; the second takes C6 paraffins overhead from naphthenes and heavier components.
Restore the best three-column design before making targeted adjustments; the latest C5 cut lost too much saleable product.
Rebuild around four direct blend cuts with much lower duties: C3/C4, C4/C5, C5/C6, and C6-paraffin/heavy. This avoids selling any unsaleable intermediate while sharply reducing column cost.
Sharpen the valuable C6-paraffin/naphthene split and move more N-hexane overhead; a saleable paraffin blend should justify the added duty.

Focus on the easiest high-value product first: a sharp C5/C6 feed split followed by C4/C5 removal should yield a saleable C5 blend with only two columns. Higher pressure avoids severe refrigeration costs.
Rebuild around the two valuable, forgiving blend products: recover a clean C5 blend overhead and a C6-paraffin blend from the heavy branch, while leaving low-value lights and heavies unsold.
Cut equipment and energy costs sharply while adding the easy C3/C4 split. Lower the C5-column boil-up to keep butane out of its overhead blend.

Build a four-column train targeting the three highest-value blend products: C5, C6 paraffins, and C6 naphthenes. Use a difficult, high-resolution n-hexane/methylcyclopentane split but much cheaper adjacent splits.
Use a liquid side draw on the primary column to recover the valuable C5 blend directly, avoiding the unprofitable third column while retaining the C6-paraffin bottoms split.

Concentrate on the most valuable C6-paraffin blend: reject everything through C5 overhead, then split the C6 paraffins from naphthenes and heavier material. Remove the two low-value branches to control cost.
Use a single side-draw column to recover the valuable C5 blend directly, avoiding the very high cost of a second column.
Sharpen both cuts at roughly their current material balances: keep dimethylbutane out of the C5 feed at the root and butanes out of the C5 bottoms, aiming to unlock the large C5-blend revenue.
Drive each blend-boundary split to high recovery with stronger boil-up, remove the unprofitable heavy column, and recover the C4 blend with a C3/C4 split.
Switch to the most robust valuable product: first reject C4 and lighter material, then recover a 95%+ C5 blend overhead with two moderate columns.
Simplify to a two-column C5-blend recovery train: first remove C4 and lighter, then separate C5 from C6 and heavier. Moderate stages and reflux should control cost while producing a saleable blend.

Rebuild as a three-product blend train: first isolate C5-and-lighter from C6-plus, then split C4 from C5 and C3 from C4. Keeping the downstream columns at feed-column pressure should avoid unnecessarily cold condensers.
Sharpen all three carbon-number cuts so the C3, C4, and C5 streams reach blend purity. Higher root pressure should reduce refrigeration cost while lower boil-up keeps C5 in the bottoms.

Rebuild around clean blend boundaries: C5 overhead at the root, C4 overhead next, C6 paraffins overhead from the heavy branch, and C6 naphthenes overhead last. Reduce equipment where possible while sharpening the root and final cuts.

Return to the profitable two-column design and sharpen only the primary C4/C5 versus C6 split. Higher recovery of the valuable C5 and C6-paraffin blends should justify a moderate increase in column cost.
Sharpen both cuts so the bottoms-then-tops stream meets the 95% C6-paraffin blend specification; its roughly $1B/yr value should outweigh the two-column cost.
Restore the best three-column configuration; the latest reflux/boil-up increases nearly doubled costs without improving sales.
Concentrate all remaining value in the C6-paraffin blend using only two columns; sharpen the heavy split enough to exceed 95% while eliminating the costly light-end train.
Use three moderate columns to recover the C5 blend and high-value C6 paraffin blend; force C5 overhead in the second column and split hexane from naphthenes in the third.
Restore the best valid two-column C5-blend design after the nonconverged simplification, then use its detailed column results to tune the cut and operating cost.
Focus on the highest-value recoverable product: keep the established C5/C6 split, discard the low-value light branch, and isolate the C6 paraffin blend from the heavy stream.
Increase vapour traffic enough to recover all C4 overhead at the root and all C5 overhead from B, while sharpening the C3/C4 cut. This should finally make the C4 and C5 blends saleable.
Concentrate on the three valuable C5/C6 blends: drive essentially all C5 overhead at the root, remove the uneconomic C3 branch, and push the naphthenes overhead from the heavy column.
Restore the profitable two-column design before making targeted improvements to recovery and column cost.
Move the first cut above the C6 paraffins by taking essentially all C5 and lighter overhead; then the second tops can approach the valuable 95% C6-paraffin blend.
Retarget the single column to the much more valuable C6-paraffin blend: C5 and lighter overhead, a 30% middle cut, and naphthenes/heavies in the bottoms.
Add a dedicated C5 finishing column: recover the pentane blend overhead while rejecting dimethylbutane and heavier material to the bottoms.
Reduce the second column's boil-up to reject cyclohexane and heavier contaminants from the C6-paraffin distillate. This should cross the 95% blend threshold while also cutting energy cost.
Reset to a compact two-column C5 recovery train: take C5 and lighter overhead at the feed, then reject C4 and lighter in the second column to sell the C5 blend.
Rebuild the simplest saleable C5-blend train at full feed pressure, avoiding valve losses and refrigeration. Use moderate internals to control the expensive energy and capital costs.
Recover the valuable C5 blend from the currently unsold light overhead with a C4/C5 split; the moderate settings should keep this added column affordable.
Push the remaining C4 overhead at the root, recover more C5 in the second column, and reduce C4 leakage into the C3 product. All three cuts should then meet blend purity.
Eliminate the two downstream columns whose outlets are unsaleable. This retains the valuable C6 paraffin blend while removing $223M/yr of column cost.
Reduce both columns' size and reflux while preserving the two blend cuts; the current C6 product is just above its purity threshold, so large separation margins are unnecessary.

Return to the lowest-cost configuration and optimize a single three-way column: reject C5 and lighter overhead, take C6 paraffins as a liquid side cut, and leave naphthenes and heavier components in the bottoms.

Return to the two-column C5-blend recovery, but use materially smaller, lower-duty columns than the earlier attempts. The first removes C4 and lighter material and the second splits C5 from C6; a clean C5 blend should be worth roughly $600M/yr.
Increase the C5 finishing column’s boil-up to recover the large amount of N-pentane currently lost in TBB, with modest extra stages and reflux to keep dimethylbutane below the blend limit.
Switch to the compact three-blend flowsheet that discards only the low-value light ends: recover the C5 blend, then the high-value C6-paraffin blend, with moderate duties.
Concentrate on the robust, valuable C5 blend: an easy C4/C5 split followed by a high-boil-up C5/C6 split, with lower stages and reflux to control cost.

Sharpen both cuts while reducing boil-up so the first tops excludes C5 and the second tops is a nearly pure C5 blend. The C5 pool is valuable enough to justify more separation if both columns converge.
Return to the profitable two-column design and try a liquid middle cut on the main column to recover the valuable C5 blend without paying for a third column.

Discard the unsold heavy branch and cut the cost of the only profitable C4 train. Higher operating pressure and fewer stages should sharply reduce refrigeration, equipment, and energy costs while retaining the C3/C4 blend split.
Reduce the C6 paraffin splitter’s size and duties while retaining enough separation for 95% blend purity.
Restore the best two-column blend flowsheet, then use the remaining budget for targeted purity and cost improvements.
Reduce vapour traffic substantially to place the first cut between C4 and C5 and the second between C5 and C6. Smaller columns and lower duties should make the C5 blend profitable.
Sharpen the C5 finishing split and drive more N-pentane overhead while keeping dimethylbutane in the bottoms; the large unsold TBB stream still contains substantial recoverable value.
Target the two highest-value blends directly: first reject C4 and lighter, then take a pure C5 distillate, and finally split C6 paraffins from naphthenes and heavier material.
Remove the unproductive heavy-end column and use the existing overhead to make the valuable C5 blend; this easy isobutane/isopentane split should yield C4 overhead and a saleable C5 bottoms stream.
Raise boil-up sharply on both cuts: the C4/C5 column must drive residual butane overhead, and the C5/C6 column must exclude that butane from the saleable C5 tops.
The side draw destroys both blend purities and is uneconomic. Restore the best two-column design, then use its measured stream compositions for a targeted improvement.
Run the two-column C4 train at full feed pressure to eliminate refrigeration, with shorter columns and enough vapour traffic to sell the C3 and C4 blends.
Revert the failed cost reduction and recover the best valid two-column C6 paraffin design before targeted tuning.
Increase boil-up to recover more N-hexane into the C6-paraffin product while slightly reducing reflux and stages to control cost.
Retarget the single three-way column to a C5 side product: take C4 and lighter overhead and leave C6 and heavier in the bottoms.

Sharpen both cuts around the C5 blend with enough boil-up to eliminate the large C4 leakage and C6 carryover. This targets about $618M/yr of blend revenue, which can support moderately larger columns.
Increase the C5 finishing column’s boil-up and separation capacity to recover more of the 178 mol/s of N-pentane currently lost in TBB while retaining dimethylbutane in the bottoms.
Use the final solves on a simple, robust two-column C6-paraffin recovery scheme. Strong C5/C6 and C6/heavy cuts should produce a high-value blend with revenue well above the column costs.
The C4/C5 split is close but reflux-limited. Increase rectification and boil-up in the smaller second column to obtain a saleable C5 blend while leaving the effective first split unchanged.
Drastically reduce internals and reflux in the two-column C5-blend train; the previous tall columns cost more than the product is worth.

The profitable design is over-purifying a blend that needs only 95% purity. Reduce both columns' stages and reflux to cut the very large capital and energy costs while retaining the C6-paraffin product.
Restore moderate pressure on the compact C3/C4 train to recover convergence while retaining low equipment and refrigeration costs.
Recover the valuable C5 blend from the light overhead by sharpening the root C5/C6 boundary and adding a moderate-duty C4/C5 splitter; retain the proven C6 paraffin branch.
Restore the best two-column blend design, then inspect its stream compositions and costs for targeted improvements.
Move the liquid side draw above the feed to the C5-rich region, keeping the same low-cost one-column configuration and total C5 draw rate.
Reduce vapour traffic at both cuts: the present settings carry most C5 into the first overhead and substantial C6 into the second overhead. Target a clean C4/C5 split followed by a clean C5/C6 split.
Recover the large C4 stream as a saleable C4 blend in TT bottoms, sending ethane and the C3s overhead; this uses an otherwise worthless 849 mol/s stream.
Use the final solve for a single-column C6-paraffin side draw, rejecting C5-and-lighter overhead and naphthenes-plus-heavier in the bottoms to avoid all downstream column cost.
Split C4 and lighter overhead at the feed, then recover the C5 blend overhead from the large bottoms stream. Lower pressure should reduce refrigeration cost while moderate stages control capital.
Try a single-column C5 recovery with a liquid side draw. If the middle cut meets blend purity, this avoids the very high capital and energy cost of the two-column train.
Restore the profitable two-column baseline before making a targeted, low-cost recovery of the valuable C5 blend from its light overhead.
Restore the best valid design; the current two-column train remains loss-making and the remaining solves are insufficient to establish a profitable separation train.
Return to the best two-column C6-paraffin design, then use the remaining budget only for modest tuning around its profitable operating point.
Add a relatively lean C4/C5 column to recover the large C5 blend value from the light overhead, while retaining the proven C6-paraffin split.
Use two moderate-duty columns to recover both valuable C5 and C6-paraffin blends: reject C4 and lighter overhead, then take C5 overhead, C6 paraffins as a liquid side cut, and heavies in the bottoms.
Restore the best valid single-column side-draw design before making a more economical final attempt.
Test a modestly higher C5 finishing boil-up to recover more N-pentane overhead while watching the 95% blend-purity limit.
Keep nearly all C5 in the feed-column bottoms, then move the second column's cut upward to between C5 and C6. This should turn the currently unsaleable BT stream into a valuable C5 blend.
Add a targeted C4/C5 splitter on the light overhead to recover the valuable C5 blend, using moderate size and lower pressure to keep the added cost controlled.
Reduce the root column’s expensive size and duties while preserving its C5/C6 cut; the downstream C6 blend splitter remains unchanged so its purity response isolates the savings opportunity.
Sharpen the C4/C5 split substantially: both outlet blends are close enough in composition that a higher-resolution column should unlock their large combined value.
Make a clean C5/C6 split first, then recover the C6 paraffins as the second column's tops; remove the unproductive side draw.
Continue the successful C5 finishing trend: a modest boil-up increase should recover more N-pentane overhead while retaining enough margin below the blend purity limit.
Try a single-column three-way cut: C4 and lighter overhead, a liquid C5-rich side draw, and C6+ bottoms. This avoids the costly second column while targeting the valuable C5 blend.
Sharpen the single-column three-way cut: much higher boil-up should expel residual C4 from the side draw, while the higher liquid side-draw stage targets the C5 blend.
Tighten the C4/C5 split so the valuable C5 blend reaches 95% purity; the current moderate splitter recovers the blend flow but leaves 14% butane contamination.
Make one final low-capital, no-refrigeration attempt at the two-column C4-blend train; if it remains loss-making, retain the empty design.
Trim the C6 splitter’s reflux and stages while retaining boil-up for recovery, aiming to preserve blend purity with substantially lower operating and capital cost.
Restore the proven C6-paraffin design and target only C5-bottoms purity: much higher boil-up should expel N-butane, while fewer stages and lower reflux limit the added column's cost.
Set the two product splits by material balance: all C5 and lighter overhead, then a C6-paraffin tops product. Lower reflux with adequate stages should control the very high energy cost.
Try a compact, low-duty single-column C5 side cut. The draw is below the feed stage and sized to the C5 flow, minimizing refrigeration and vapour traffic.
Use the remaining budget on the two proven recovery opportunities: more N-pentane overhead in the C5 finisher and more C4 into the saleable TT bottoms, while checking both 95% blend limits.
Target the much more valuable C6-paraffin blend instead: reject C5 and lighter overhead at the feed, then take the four paraffins overhead from methylcyclopentane and heavier material.

A single three-way column is the cheapest potential route to the valuable C5 blend. Increase rectification and stripping substantially while keeping full feed pressure to test whether the side cut can reach 95%.
Make the C4/C5 splitter much cheaper and operate it near atmospheric pressure, where the volatility gap should let the C5 blend exceed 95% without the current excessive size and reflux.
Restore the profitable two-column C6-paraffin design; the latest trim destroyed both saleable products and is uneconomic.
Increase C4/C5 boil-up to recover more high-value isopentane into the C5 blend while retaining the current split and stage count.
Increase separation efficiency at the two blend cuts: the present train loses substantial C5 overhead and C6 paraffins into the wrong products, so zero revenue cannot justify its cost.
Restore the best turn-19 design; both recovery increases in turn 20 reduced net profit, so the previous C4 and C5 operating points are preferable.
Use one lower-cost three-way column to recover the valuable C6-paraffin blend as a side draw, rejecting C5 and lighter overhead and naphthenes/heavier in the bottoms.

Return to the best single-column concept but cut capital sharply: 30 stages with enough stripping to keep C4 out of the C5 side draw. This targets positive margin rather than incremental purity at very high cost.
The light-product branch remains uneconomic. Restore the profitable two-column baseline and then tune one column at a time to reduce cost without losing blend purity.
Test a higher root operating pressure to reduce refrigeration and utility cost while keeping the proven C5/C6 split and downstream settings unchanged.
Split the light stream first as C3 versus C4/C5, then recover both the C4 and C5 blends in one additional column; this monetizes the large unsold overhead while keeping the proven C6 split.

Recover the high-value C6-paraffin blend with two direct cuts: C5 and lighter overhead first, then C6 paraffins overhead from the naphthenes and heavier components. Moderate reflux and boil-up are matched to the expected product flows.
Reduce the C5 finishing column from 75 to 60 stages at its best operating point; its current product has purity margin, so this may cut substantial capital cost without losing sales.
Recover the two highest-value remaining blends: split C6+ from the feed, separate the four C6 paraffins from naphthenes, then recover the C6 naphthene blend from C7+.

Rebuild the C5-blend train with moderate internals: an easy C4/C5 split followed by a sharper C5/C6 split. This targets about $620M/yr of blend revenue without the excessive duties of earlier attempts.

Reduce only the C6-paraffin recovery column’s size and reflux while preserving its split. The current product has just over 95% blend purity, so this tests whether most of its $336M/yr cost is unnecessary.
